reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An acute, usually self-limiting hypersensitivity reaction characterised by target (iris) lesions with three concentric zones
Lesions are typically symmetrical and acral, favouring the extensor surfaces of the hands, forearms, feet, and often the palms and soles
Herpes simplex virus is the commonest trigger, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an important cause, particularly in children
Erythema multiforme major involves significant mucosal disease (oral, ocular, or genital) in addition to skin lesions, whereas the minor form has little or no mucosal involvement
It is now regarded as distinct from Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which have different triggers (mainly drugs), morphology, and far greater skin detachment and mortality
Management is largely supportive with removal or treatment of the trigger; recurrent herpes-associated disease may warrant suppressive antiviral therapy
Recurrent or persistent disease should prompt a search for an underlying herpes infection or other trigger
reference.pathophysiology: Erythema multiforme is a cell-mediated immune reaction, most often provoked by infection, in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes target keratinocytes expressing antigens derived from the trigger. In herpes-associated disease, viral DNA fragments are transported to the skin and drive a T-cell response with interferon-gamma-mediated inflammation at the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic target lesions with central epidermal damage. This immunopathology and its infective triggers distinguish it from the drug-driven, tumour-necrosis-factor and granulysin-mediated widespread keratinocyte apoptosis of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic target lesions and distribution
Testing for herpes simplex virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae when a trigger is sought
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to distinguish from other reactions
Review of recent medications to help differentiate from drug-induced severe reactions
Assessment of mucosal and ocular involvement, with ophthalmology input where indicated
redFlags: Extensive skin detachment or a positive Nikolsky sign suggesting Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis
Severe mucosal involvement impairing oral intake, vision, or urination
Systemic upset with fever and mucosal disease requiring urgent assessment
Ocular involvement threatening long-term visual complications
reference.prognosis: Erythema multiforme minor is generally self-limiting and resolves over a few weeks without scarring; the herpes-associated form is prone to recurrence, and prognosis is far better than for the more severe drug-induced blistering syndromes it must be distinguished from.
pitfalls: Confusing erythema multiforme with Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis and mismanaging severity
Overlooking an underlying herpes simplex or Mycoplasma trigger, especially in recurrent disease
Failing to assess and manage mucosal and ocular involvement
Attributing a target-like drug eruption to infection and missing a culprit medication
management: Identification and treatment of the trigger, using aciclovir for herpes simplex-associated disease and an appropriate macrolide or other antibiotic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Withdrawal of any suspected culprit drug
Symptomatic skin care with topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines and analgesia for the target lesions
Mucosal care with antiseptic and anaesthetic mouthwashes, with attention to hydration where oral involvement limits intake
Ophthalmology review and treatment for ocular mucosal involvement to prevent scarring
Continuous suppressive antiviral therapy for recurrent herpes-associated disease
Supportive care with monitoring to distinguish from and detect evolution toward the more severe drug-induced blistering syndromes
